newsitem.title: FINLAND: U.S., Russia strike arms accords at summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russia strike arms accords at summit.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin built on their post-Cold War partnership with a series of arms agreements on Friday, including the promise of more cuts in nuclear arsenals.

At their summit in Helsinki, Yeltsin promised to push the Russian Duma (parliament) to finally ratify the long-stalled START-2 strategic arms reduction treaty, which was signed in 1993, and expressed confidence that he would succeed.

The two leaders, in a joint statement, also agreed that once START-2 enters into force, they would move immediately to negotiate a follow-on pact that would take long-range nuclear arms down to about 20 percent of their Cold War levels.

Most surprisingly, U.S. officials said, the two presidents late in their summit settled a long-running dispute over the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (ABM) and can now each develop theatre missile defences to tackle new threats.

Less dramatic but crucial to allaying Russian fears about NATO expansion, the summit's central focus, was an agreement to speed negotiations on new cuts in conventional forces in Europe with the aim of a framework pact in the next few months.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called it a "major summit (with) historic progress," including on arms.

Compromise was required but General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, dismissed talk of U.S. concessions. Decisions made were in the country's "best national security interests", he said.

American arms control expert Jack Mendelsohn said the progress appeared significant. But he was not as confident as Yeltsin about the Russian Duma ratifying START-2 and he said there may still be problems with the ABM accord.
Most of the focus at Helsinki was on Yeltsin's decision to sign a charter defining Russia's relations with NATO by the time alliance leaders meet in July to decide on new members.
The charter is seen as a crucial mechanism tying Russia to European security decisions into the next century and calming Moscow's fears about an enlarged NATO someday turning hostile.
But the arms control issues were a critical subtext because they affect Russia's perspective of its security and because Moscow had tied charter discussions to arms issues.
START-2 was ratified by the U.S. Senate but the Duma, dominated by Yeltsin's nationalist and communist opponents, has refused to do so because of opposition to NATO expansion and other concerns.

Under START-2, U.S. and Russian arsenals would be reduced by the year 2003 to 3,500 deployed warheads per side, compared to the 6,000 per side warhead target under the first START agreement, now in force.
A new START-3 agreement, if achieved, would aim for levels of 2,000 to 2,500 warheads each by the year 2007.
Arms experts say Russia would have to spend money it simply does not have to ensure its arsenal stays on a par with the United States.

As a result, Washington agreed to move quickly to START-3 negotiations and to give Russia four more years to dismantle silos, bombers and submarines under START-2. It also gave Moscow an extra year to dismantle nuclear warheads.
Mendelsohn said the date change was significant because it gave Russia 10 years to evaluate the impact on its security of NATO expansion and the missile defence accord.
Washington and Moscow negotiated for more than three years on what theatre missile defence systems would be allowed under the ABM treaty.
